concerns.text: FR-007 is not anchored to any user story; it only references “Edge Cases”. It should explicitly reference the relevant story (e.g., US‑1) or be merged into an existing requirement.
FR-008 lacks a story anchor; it only mentions “Edge Cases”. Add a reference to the appropriate user story (likely US‑1) or integrate it with a related requirement.
FR-009 is orphaned – it cites only “Edge Cases” and does not name a user story. Provide an explicit trace to the story it serves (e.g., US‑1) or consolidate it with another requirement.
SC-006 references “Edge Cases” but does not tie to a specific user story. Anchor it to the story whose scope it validates (e.g., US‑1) or re‑word to make the linkage clear.
SC-007 is similarly orphaned, only citing “Edge Cases”. It should be linked to the appropriate user story (likely US‑1) or merged with a related success criterion.

Functional Requirements reference undefined identifiers ‘US‑1’, ‘US‑2’, ‘US‑3’ (e.g., “(See US‑1)”). No user‑story IDs with this naming exist in the document; the stories are labeled ‘User Story 1’, ‘User Story 2’, etc. This breaks traceability and creates a dangling cross‑reference.

Success Criteria SC‑004 mentions reporting a global‑context activation proportion “≤ X %” for failure cases and “≥ Y %” for success cases, but the concrete values X and Y are never defined elsewhere in the spec, leaving the requirement underspecified.

The validation target 'global‑context activation proportion' (SC‑004) is directly determined by the sparsity configuration that masks global‑context tokens (FR‑005). When the attention window is reduced, the masked tokens cannot receive activation, making the proportion trivially low. Thus the metric is not independent of the predictor, resulting in a circular validation of the very effect the experiment aims to measure.

SC‑003 proposes computing Pearson (and optionally Spearman) correlations between the numeric 'window size' (0, 64, 32, 16, 1) and mIoU. Window size is a categorical treatment of attention sparsity, not a continuous variable; treating it as numeric can produce misleading correlation coefficients. A more appropriate analysis would use an ordered‑factor trend test (e.g., Jonckheere‑Terpstra) or a mixed‑effects regression that respects the categorical nature of the predictor.
